meta.title: I Think AI Could Replace 80% of Knowledge Work Jobs. And I Believe We Need to Prepare Now.
meta.seoTitle: AI and Jobs: Preparing for the Future
meta.description: Why I worry about extensive automation of knowledge work, what the research says and how to think through a personal strategy for the years ahead.
meta.excerpt: The 80% figure is my hypothesis, not a statistic. Here is why I take this risk seriously and how I want to help people think about their future.

content.text: We may be at the beginning of an economic and social transformation far greater than we realise. Here is why I think the next ten years could reshape our relationship with work, and why I decided to create a tool to help people think about their future.

sections.title: A conviction that may sound extreme

content.text: I will start with a fairly radical claim:
I think that, within five to ten years, artificial intelligence could make up to 80% of today’s knowledge work jobs carried out mainly at a computer redundant.
That figure does not come from a study. It is my personal hypothesis, and I do not claim I can prove it today.

I am a developer. I work with these technologies, use them to build applications and see how quickly they improve. The more I use them, the harder I find it to imagine our workplaces continuing as they are.

Just a few years ago, developing an application took weeks or months of work. Today, some tasks that used to take several days can be completed in minutes. That does not apply everywhere yet, mistakes still happen and complexity has not disappeared. But I find the direction of travel hard to ignore.
Above all, I see no reason to assume that progress will simply stop where it is today.

sections.title: The real upheaval will be economic

content.text: AI is often presented as a tool that will make us more productive. That is true. But I think the discussion too often stops at that first consequence.

Imagine a company employing ten people to deliver a digital service. With AI, perhaps three people could soon do the same work, or more. The company would then have several options: produce more, lower its prices, develop new services… or reduce its workforce.

Some people believe higher productivity will create enough new activity to offset the jobs lost. That is possible. Economic history has already shown that innovation can create occupations nobody anticipated.
But something feels different to me this time:
AI is not just replacing individual tasks. It is making progress in the very abilities we use to learn, reason, create and devise solutions.
If new occupations emerge, what guarantees that they will not quickly be automated too?
Even if companies keep their employees, they could simply stop hiring as many people. Unemployment would then come not only from redundancies, but also from opportunities gradually disappearing.
There are already signs worth watching. In August 2026, a
Stanford study

found that employment among Americans aged 22 to 25 in the occupations most exposed to AI was around 19% below where it would have been had it kept pace with less exposed occupations. This is a relative gap, not 19% of jobs eliminated by AI. The researchers stress that their data cannot establish how much of this gap was caused by generative AI, nor support a conclusion of widespread job displacement across the economy.
In France, a
Coface study published on 17 November 2026
also observes job postings falling behind in the most exposed occupations, without being able to establish a definite causal link.
These studies do not prove my 80% scenario. But they show that the question is no longer purely theoretical.

sections.title: A society that could become far more unequal

content.text: What worries me most is not just the disappearance of certain jobs. It is the possible consequences for society as a whole.

In an economy where automated systems handled a growing share of production, who would capture the productivity gains? Employees? Consumers through lower prices? Or mainly companies and the owners of these technologies?

I fear wealth could become increasingly concentrated. On one side, people able to own businesses, products, infrastructure or capital. On the other, a growing number of people whose skills had lost some of their economic value.
The
International Monetary Fund
has already identified this risk: AI could increase wealth inequality by raising returns on capital. The scale of that effect will depend in part on how the gains are distributed.

I also fear greater social and political polarisation. If some people see their career prospects deteriorate while others rapidly grow wealthier, trust in our institutions could come under severe strain. That could lead to more insecurity, social tension, resentment and political instability.
None of this is inevitable. Public policy, redistribution, training and social protections will play a substantial role.
Other projections are more optimistic: in 2025, the
World Economic Forum
projected a net increase of 78 million jobs by 2030, based on surveyed employers’ expectations and taking several major economic transformations into account, not just AI.
But I would rather consider a difficult scenario and prepare for it than rely entirely on society absorbing this transition without too much damage.

sections.title: I do not want to wait until the problem affects me personally

content.text: Faced with this prospect, it would be easy to feel powerless. What can one person do about such a large transformation? I think that is precisely why we need to start thinking now.
Not necessarily to change jobs tomorrow, and certainly not to rush into abandoning a career built over years. But to ask a question we have rarely needed to consider this seriously:
If my professional skills lost much of their value over the next ten years, what could I rely on to keep making a decent living?

For some, the answer might be to develop expertise in a field that is harder to automate. For others, it could mean becoming self-employed, building assets, developing a product or acquiring skills tied to the physical world.

There is probably no universal strategy. Someone who enjoys starting businesses, taking risks and selling their services will not have the same options as someone who values stability above all, prefers working alone and hates looking for customers.
That is exactly what made me want to create a tool.

sections.title: A tool for thinking through your own strategy

content.text: I wondered whether it would be possible to help people step back and reflect on how they work, their motivations and their preferences, then suggest directions to explore over the coming years. The idea is neither to predict their future nor to tell them which occupation to choose, but to introduce possibilities they might not have considered.
I designed a questionnaire to build a personal and professional profile from closed-ended questions.

It explores several dimensions: how we reason, our relationship with creativity, our ability to learn, our need for autonomy, our preferences for interacting with others, and our attitudes towards entrepreneurship, financial risk and stability.
For example, do you enjoy building projects? Are you comfortable with uncertainty? Do you prefer working alone or in a team? Do you like selling? How much does control over your time matter to you?
These questions may seem far removed from artificial intelligence. Yet the answers can make a substantial difference to the strategies worth considering.

Take two examples. A creative, independent person drawn to entrepreneurship but uncomfortable with selling might explore building a small product that generates recurring revenue, perhaps with a partner whose skills complement their own.

Someone else who enjoys human interaction and practical activities might consider gradually moving into an occupation combining local relationships, technical skills and hands-on work. Both people are responding to the same risk, but their strategies may be very different.
The questionnaire offers a short version with 40 questions and an in-depth version with 80 questions.
An algorithm analyses your stated preferences and offers
five directions: a common foundation for everyone and four strategies selected from a catalogue
. Each strategy comes with an explanation: why it might suit the profile, what its advantages and limitations would be, and which first steps could be considered.

I deliberately chose a deterministic system rather than AI-generated recommendations. The rules are defined in advance: the same answers produce the same results. The aim is to offer a consistent, understandable starting point.

The questionnaire is not a scientifically validated psychological test. It does not know your actual skills, your full financial situation or the opportunities available in your sector. It therefore cannot determine what will work for you.
The aim is to help you structure your thinking and explore several options without having to start from a blank page.

The financial foundation is suggested to everyone: it does not describe your actual circumstances. If your answers are too neutral or uncertain, the tool says so and offers four general directions instead of a personalised ranking. You can save your progress on this device and resume later in French or English.

sections.title: The goal is not to become irreplaceable

content.text: One idea often comes up in discussions about artificial intelligence: we should develop skills that machines will never be able to replace. Personally, I am not convinced this is the best approach.

First, because we do not really know what these systems will be capable of in ten years. Second, because a skill can remain useful while losing a great deal of its value in the labour market. Being excellent at your job does not guarantee that a company will still need to pay as many people to do it.
I prefer to think about it differently: rather than focusing only on becoming irreplaceable, why not try to become gradually less dependent on our ability to sell our labour?

That could involve owning assets, developing an additional source of income, learning to use AI effectively, building a professional reputation, maintaining a network or having skills that transfer across several sectors.

These are possibilities, not guarantees. A product can fail, an investment can lose value and a career change can prove difficult. But developing more options can help us avoid depending on a single outcome.

sections.title: In ten years, I would like to know I planned ahead

content.text: I may be wrong about the scale of this transformation. Perhaps AI will create far more jobs than it destroys. Perhaps progress will slow down. Perhaps we will collectively find new economic balances. I hope we do.

But if my scenario comes close to reality, people who started thinking and diversifying their options today could have valuable room to manoeuvre. I do not want to wait until I face this situation personally before I start asking the right questions.
I think we are living through a major transition, and the next five to ten years could profoundly change how we work, earn a living and organise society.
The question I want to ask therefore goes beyond choosing an occupation:
“How can I build a position today that will let me retain some freedom, even if the world of work changes radically?”
That is the reflection I would like to encourage with this article and this tool.
